summary: A white paper discussing accounting requirements for IPng. It recommends that all IPng packets carry accounting tags, which would vary in size. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This white paper proposes adding accounting tags to IPng packets. A tag could identify the party responsible for a packet, and another could carry higher-layer accounting information.

questions: how to bill for network traffic
what is an ipng accounting tag
subtitle: A proposal to carry accounting information in IPng packets.

tldr.problem: The memo seeks a simpler way to identify who is responsible for packets and to carry accounting information through a network.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes variable-size accounting tags in IPng packets: a voucher for lower-layer accounting and, when needed, a separate tag for higher-layer variables.
tldr.outcome: It recommends that IPng be able to carry one or two variable-size accounting objects in each packet, with details left for later standardization.

today: RFC 1672 is Informational. It records a proposal for carrying accounting information in IPng packets, not an adopted packet format.

sections.title: Why Put Accounting Tags in Packets
sections.content:
The RFC discusses accounting requirements for IPng and builds on the Internet Accounting Model in RFC 1272. It refers to a proposal for authenticated source, destination, and transaction information in IPng packets, and calls the transaction information an accounting tag.

The memo recommends tags that can identify the party responsible for a packet and, in some cases, carry other accounting variables.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal puts accounting information in packets so network meters can use it. The simplest tag identifies who is responsible for a packet.

sections.title: How the Tags Could Be Used
sections.content:
At the network layer, a tag would act as a voucher: an arbitrary string identifying the party willing to pay for a packet. The originating host would set it, and routing policy could change it along the path to reflect a change in responsibility.

At session or application layers, a tag could carry accounting variables for meters and could help an application inform a client about resource use or charges. The memo says a gateway meter could set tag values for applications that do not know about the tag field.
sections.plainLanguage: A voucher tag could identify who pays as a packet crosses networks. A separate tag could carry information about resource use for an application or meter.

sections.title: One or Two Variable-Size Objects
sections.content:
The memo suggests keeping the voucher as part of the routing tuple and using a separate tag for application variables. This separation would keep router and meter management distinct. If encryption or digital-signature overhead for a second tag proved too high, the tags could be combined.

The RFC leaves the detailed format and packing of variables for later standardization. For IPng, it says only that the packet should be able to carry one or two variable-size objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not define the tags' exact encoding. It proposes that IPng packets have room for one or two variable-size accounting objects.

sections.title: Protecting Accounting Information
sections.content: The RFC says routing and accounting information must be tamper-proof for reliable transport in a hostile environment. Routers and meters that use the information need appropriate keys, and network operators must plan which routers need which keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Accounting tags must be protected against changes. Routers and meters need keys to check the information they use.

references.text: Mills, C., Hirchert, D., and G. Ruth, "Internet Accounting: Background", RFC 1272, November 1991.
Carpenter, B., "IPng White Paper on Transition and Other Considerations", RFC 1671, August 1994.
